content.readme:
Craft Anything

English · 日本語 · 简体中文 · 한국어

See how any website, app or game works, then have AI build your own version; an open-source, clean-room engine in pure Rust.
Point it at a target, say what you want, and it studies the original with real inspection tools,
has a coding agent build a new project, checks the result against the original and refines it.

Download Craft Anything · ArtCraft · All Crafting Apps



A website project: each check says how alike the build is, you approve anything outside the rules, and the plan shows what's left.

> [!NOTE] > **ArtCraft is a community of artists from all walks of life.** Painters, photographers, > filmmakers, illustrators, designers, animators, hobbyists, and people who picked up a pencil > last week. If you make things, you're one of us. **[Come say hi on Discord](https://discord.gg/artcraft).**

How it works · Two ways to use it · AI · Agents · Under the hood · Get started · Status · Downloads · Discord


🔍 Study anything

Websites, desktop apps, phone apps, games and files: real inspection tools find out how they're built and what they do, with the evidence behind every answer.

🛠️ Build your own

Say what you want ("Recreate this website", "Recreate this game's gameplay in Rust") and a coding agent builds a new project in the stack you ask for.

✅ Checked, not guessed

Every build is compared with the original (pages at three screen widths, a game's own self-test, an app's runs) and refined until it's close.

🤖 Agent-ready

320 tools, each one a CLI command and an MCP tool, so any agent can drive the same engine the app uses. No AI is needed to inspect.

## How it works Point Craft Anything at a target, say what you want, and press Start. It works in four steps, asking you in plain words when a decision is yours: 1. **Study:** inspect the original: its pages at every width, its code, its files, how it runs. 2. **Build:** a coding agent builds a new project, in the language, framework or engine your request names (or a sensible default). 3. **Check:** compare the build with the original and list what doesn't match yet. 4. **Ready:** open, play or preview the result, or ask for changes and it refines it.

basic_info.description: Metal driver for NVIDIA GeForce cards on macOS Sequoia

content.readme:
# NullMoth NVIDIA Driver for macOS

A Metal driver for NVIDIA GeForce cards on macOS 15 Sequoia (Intel Macs and OpenCore PCs). It is open source; the
kernel extensions, the Metal plugin and the shader translator are in this repository. The 1401 app that installs it
(Mac and Windows) is its own project: [1401](https://github.com/nullmoth/1401).

Supported cards are Turing and newer: GTX 16, RTX 20, 30, 40 and 50, TITAN RTX, Quadro RTX and the T-series. Most
testing is done on an RTX 5060, so other cards may have problems that haven't been found yet. See
[card support](docs/CARD-SUPPORT.md) for what has been reported working.

- Changes: [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md), downloads on the [releases page](https://github.com/nullmoth/nvidia-macos-driver/releases)
- Problems: [troubleshooting](docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md), then Send logs from the 1401 app
- Installing macOS from Windows: [1401](https://github.com/nullmoth/1401)
- How it works: [docs/HOW-IT-WORKS.md](docs/HOW-IT-WORKS.md)
- Contributing: [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md)

If your PC doesn't boot macOS with OpenCore yet, set that up first with the
[OpenCore Install Guide](https://dortania.github.io/OpenCore-Install-Guide/), then install the driver.

Support the work: https://buymeacoffee.com/nullmoth

| | |
|---|---|
| macOS | 15.5 Sequoia or later (tested 15.7.x and 15.8.1), or 26 Tahoe, x86_64 |
| GPUs | NVIDIA Turing and later; developed on an RTX 5060 |
| Metal | Metal 3: argument buffers tier 2, ray tracing, mesh shaders, MPS, MetalFX path |
| Also | OpenGL (through Apple's GL-on-Metal), OpenCL, Core Image, Core ML |

## How it works

```
Metal app ─► NVMTLDriver.bundle ─► translator (Apple AIR → SPIR-V) ─► NVK (Mesa Vulkan + NAK compiler) ─► kexts ─► GPU
```

| Component | Path on disk | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Metal driver plugin | `/Library/GPUBundles/NVMTLDriver.bundle` | `plugin/` |
| Shader translator | inside the plugin (`libnvmtl_translate.dylib`) | `translator/` (LGPL-3.0, based on metal2vulkan) |
| Vulkan back end (NVK) | `/Library/GPUBundles/nvmtl/` | `nvk/nvk-macos.patch` on Mesa `17ca6174` |
| Kernel extensions | `/Library/Extensions/NVRM, NVAccel, NVRMFB, NVRMAGDC` | `kexts/` |
| GPU firmware (GSP) | `/Library/NullMoth/nvfw/nvidia/615.78.08` | NVIDIA, unmodified |

The kernel side runs NVIDIA's own open GPU kernel modules (r610) under macOS. NVRMFB is the display framebuffer,
NVAccel the accelerator WindowServer composites through, NVRMAGDC the display-policy shim.

## Install — by hand

Use the 1401 Mac app below unless you manage your OpenCore config yourself. `install.sh` installs the driver files but
does not change OpenCore, and the driver does not start until OpenCore has these settings:

- `boot-args` include `nvfb=1 nvaccel=1 nvfbheads=4 -nvkmsnosmooth amfi_get_out_of_my_way=0x1 amfi=0x80
  ipc_control_port_options=0`, and not `nv_disable=1` or `-wegnoegpu` (both hide the NVIDIA card)
- `csr-active-config` includes the bits `0x0A43`
- `Misc > Security > SecureBootModel` is `Disabled`
- `Lilu.kext` and `AMFIPass.kext` are in `Kernel > Add` and enabled

Download `nullmoth-nvidia-<version>.tar.gz` from **Releases**, then:

```bash
tar -xzf nullmoth-nvidia-*.tar.gz && cd pkgroot
shasum -a 256 -c SHA256SUMS
sudo ./install.sh
sudo shutdown -r now
```

Every file must say OK in the check. `install.sh` copies the files and rebuilds the Auxiliary Kernel Collection; the
restart is required, because logging out does not load the driver. (Paste the lines without anything after them: the
Terminal on macOS does not treat `#` as a comment, so a pasted comment becomes part of the command.)

macOS asks you to **allow the extensions** in System Settings → Privacy & Security the first time. Allow, then reboot again.

## 1401 Mac app (recommended)

Download the latest `1401-Mac-<version>.dmg` from **Releases**, open it, and run **1401** (the driver package is inside the disk
image, so nothing else to download). Follow its steps. A supported setup must use a verified or explicitly selected OpenCore partition. The app finds the OpenCore that started your Mac (in `EFI/OC` or `EFI/BOOT`, on an
EFI or FAT32 partition), shows every change before making it, backs the config up, installs the driver, and adds
**1401: Remove NVIDIA driver** to the OpenCore boot picker. Choosing that entry removes the driver at the next start and
puts the Mac back exactly as it was before the install, OpenCore config included, then restarts by itself. The app also
maps your USB ports and, if the driver ever crashes the Mac, offers to make a crash report you can upload yourself
(it never sends anything on its own).

If something goes wrong, open 1401 > Crash report > Send logs to NullMoth. It uploads what 1401 did, the driver's
state, crash reports and OpenCore's startup log, with names, serial numbers and addresses removed, and gives you a
report ID to put in your issue or in Discord.

Keep the USB stick or disk that OpenCore started from plugged in while the app runs, and f

CCBaga

English · 简体中文

A native macOS, Linux and Windows toolkit for a cleaner workspace and an environment you can verify.

Claude identities · Browser fingerprints · System settings · Network Skill

Features · Installation · Updates · Quick start · Usage guide · Architecture · Development · Contributing

![CCBaga: native control, observable environments](docs/readme-hero.png) **Intended use:** CCBaga is intended solely for people residing or traveling abroad to manage their own Claude identities. Use that violates Anthropic's official terms of service is prohibited. CCBaga brings local maintenance and environment setup into one focused desktop workflow. Inspect Claude data before removing it, rotate your companion browser's fingerprint and restart it, align system settings with a selected region, and compare real browser readings with the machine and network exit. Two applications work together: **CCBaga-A** owns native operations; **CCBaga-B** runs an isolated Fingerprint Chromium profile. Browser measurements return to the host through a local session. Changing a setting and verifying its effect are separate steps. ## Features
Local Claude identities

Archive the current local identity, switch to a saved identity or start with an empty workspace. Choose what stays shared and what moves with each identity.		 Fingerprint & restart

Generate a fresh seed, apply the selected region's language and timezone, then restart the companion browser.		 Real environment checks

Compare browser and machine readings with the actual network exit. Passing measured checks produces a green page and a large checkmark.
Native system settings

Apply timezone, preferred language and region settings. Open desktop controls for location and permissions; see platform-specific limits.		 AI-guided network setup

Three simple steps, a coding-agent selector and a copyable Skill installation prompt. Give the AI your files and connection details; it handles the commands.		 Claude Code CLI tools

Detect the installation method and version. Uninstall or reinstall through native, npm/bun, Homebrew or WinGet workflows.
**One region selector. Four everyday actions.** Easy setup puts browser cache cleanup, fingerprint rotation, timezone/language reset and identity archiving on the same page. The sidebar keeps advanced controls in Network, Claude identities, Browser and Computer. The interface supports **English and Chinese**, with shared YAML catalogs. Switching the interface language does not change the computer or browser language. The bilingual **Usage guide** covers common actions and data boundaries. See the [full guide](docs/usage.md). ## Installation **Platforms:** macOS 12 or later on Apple Silicon; Linux x86_64 with GTK 3 and WebKitGTK 4.1; Windows 10/11 x86_64. Intel macOS and Linux ARM64 are not supported. Linux x86_64 packages include DEB, RPM and AppImage built on Ubuntu 22.04 (glibc 2.35), plus a separate package for current Arch/pacman systems. All include the companion browser. See [Linux setup](docs/linux.md) for installation and platform limits. Official versions are published exclusively by the project owner, **liseami**. Windows x86_64 uses one NSIS setup installer containing both A and B. The installer is not Authenticode

# Owly https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/b195ce4c-e078-49be-bc13-44a72b6dc189 AirDrop between iPhones and Linux devices whose Wi-Fi isn't Apple's Broadcom chip. See [supported hardware](#supported-hardware). ## Install
Arch/Omarchy If using Omarchy, you can install Owly together with [omdrop](https://github.com/netmojo-systems/omdrop-plugin) to get it in your bar: ```sh # Install Omdrop: omarchy plugin add https://github.com/netmojo-systems/omdrop-plugin.git # Install Owly (omdrop-owl): yay -S omdrop-owl ``` If you're just using Arch, or don't want the UI, you can just install the CLI: ```sh yay -S owly ```
NixOS ```nix inputs.owly.url = "github:t4t5/owly"; ``` ```nix imports = [ inputs.owly.nixosModules.default ]; services.owly.enable = true; services.owly.settings = { allow_untested = true; }; ```
Debian/Ubuntu Download the `.deb` from the [releases page](https://github.com/t4t5/owly/releases) and run: ```sh sudo apt install ./owly_*_amd64.deb # Debian 12, Ubuntu 22.04 and newer ```
Fedora Download the `.rpm` from the [releases page](https://github.com/t4t5/owly/releases) and run: ```sh sudo dnf install ./owly-*.x86_64.rpm # Fedora 44 and newer ```
From source Requires Rust 1.88 or newer: ```sh cargo build --release --locked -p owlyd -p owly-cli sudo packaging/install.sh owly sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo nmcli general reload conf ```

basic_info.name: hatchzip
basic_info.description: HatchZip is a free, open-source archive extractor for Windows, macOS and Linux that extracts ZIP, 7z, RAR, tar and split archives in place, so it needs free space for the extracted files only. Desktop app and CLI.

content.readme:
HatchZip

Extract huge archives in place. The archive shrinks as your files hatch,
so you only need free space for the output, not for the output and the archive.

hatchzip.dev | Installation | Usage | Safety | How it works | Contributing

HatchZip is a free, open-source archive extractor for Windows, macOS and Linux, with a desktop app and a command line tool. It extracts ZIP, 7z, RAR, tar and split archives in place, for when there is not enough disk space to extract an archive next to itself, such as a large game download on a nearly full disk. Download it from [hatchzip.dev](https://hatchzip.dev). A 180 GB game download that unpacks to 200 GB needs 380 GB of disk with WinRAR, 7-Zip or `unzip`, because the archive and everything extracted from it have to exist at the same time. HatchZip needs a little over 200 GB. It extracts the archive from the end and cuts each finished part off the archive file as it goes, so the space the archive gives back is reused for the next files. It checks that the extraction will fit before it changes anything, keeps a safety margin of free space the whole way through, and can be stopped or crash at any moment and pick up where it left off. It reads ZIP, 7z, tar, `.tar.gz`, `.tar.xz`, RAR volume sets and split archives. ### Get it > [!IMPORTANT] > HatchZip is only distributed from this repository's [releases](https://github.com/xevrion/hatchzip/releases) and its site, [hatchzip.dev](https://hatchzip.dev). Other sites using the name, such as hatchzip.com, are not affiliated with this project. No coding needed. **[Download for Windows](https://github.com/xevrion/hatchzip/releases/latest/download/HatchZip-x64-setup.exe)** (Windows 10 and 11), or for [macOS (Apple Silicon)](https://github.com/xevrion/hatchzip/releases/latest/download/HatchZip-aarch64.dmg), [macOS (Intel)](https://github.com/xevrion/hatchzip/releases/latest/download/HatchZip-x86_64.dmg) and [Linux](#installation). 1. Run the installer. Windows may show "Windows protected your PC" because HatchZip is not code-signed yet: choose **More info**, then **Run anyway**. 2. Right-click the archive, choose **HatchZip**, then **Extract here**. On Windows 11 the menu is under **Show more options**. To pick the destination folder first, choose **Extract files…** instead. 3. Or open HatchZip from the Start menu, open the archive, and choose **Extract**. HatchZip shows whether the files will fit before it changes anything. The archive is used up as the files come out, so when it finishes, only the extracted files are left. **Extract here** puts an archive with one folder or one file at its top next to the archive. An archive with several files or folders at its top goes into a new folder named after it, so its files never mix with what is already there. The progress window closes when the extraction completes; to keep it open, clear **Close the progress window when extraction completes** in the app's Settings menu. To keep the archive when there is room for both, choose **Extract here (keep archive)** in the right-click menu. To always keep archives, as other extractors do, clear **Remove the archive during extraction** in the app's Settings menu; every right-click entry then keeps the archive too. That is a normal extraction: the archive is not changed, and space is required for all extracted files. ## When there is not enough disk space to extract The same 200 MB of game data (21 files), packed by the real tools, extracted on a 220 MiB disk with about 50 MB free: | Archive | `unzip` / 7-Zip | HatchZip | |---|---|---| | ZIP, 180 MB | `unzip` ran out of space at file 6 of 21 | Finished, every file byte-identical | | 7z from 7-Zip 25.01, `-ms=20m` (10 solid blocks) | Needs 380 MB | Finished in 0.64 s, every file byte-identical | | 7z split into 5 volumes of 40 MB | Needs 380

basic_info.name: RustGIS
basic_info.description: A fast, free and open-source GIS in pure Rust.

content.readme:
RustGIS

A fast, free and open-source GIS in pure Rust for mapping, analyzing and sharing geospatial data.
Native on Windows, macOS and Linux, and in your web browser. Your data stays on your machine unless you send it to an AI model you choose, and every action is a command you can script.

## Why RustGIS - **Fast and small.** One native program, drawn on the GPU, with no runtime to install and no server to run. - **Runs everywhere.** The same app on Windows, macOS and Linux, and compiled to WebAssembly at [web.rustgis.app](https://web.rustgis.app) with nothing to install. - **Local and private.** Your files are read and written on your machine, and nothing is uploaded on its own. The network is used only when you ask for it: web basemaps, plugins, the GeoLibre tools and the AI model you pick, which receives your questions and the data it reads to answer them. - **Everything is a command.** Every button in the ribbon is a command with an id. Script it from `rustgis-cli`, chain it in notebooks and models, use completion in the Script pane, or ask the AI Assistant to run it for you. - **Familiar.** A ribbon laid out in the order of the work (Home, Data, Style, Edit, Analyze, View, Publish), Layers and Browser panes, an attribute table, and undo for every change. - **Extensible.** Over 1,000 GeoLibre and Whitebox tools for terrain, hydrology, LiDAR and remote sensing, and sandboxed WebAssembly [plugins](docs/plugins.md) that add commands, tools and ribbon tabs. ## A tour Prefer a video? [RustGIS: A Fast, Free GIS That Runs on Your Desktop and in Your Browser](https://youtu.be/XFhqlSiKn6U) walks through the main features, and the [Video Tutorials](https://rustgis.app/videos/) page collects the rest of the [playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLBQuwPke8dNI).

Symbology and tables. Graduated colours, with the selection synced to the table.

basic_info.name: fsearch
basic_info.description: Whole-disk file search for macOS: fuzzy names, typo tolerance, indexed content grep. ~1 ms over 8M files.

content.readme:
# FSearch

Whole-disk file search for macOS: names in about 0.1 ms, typo-tolerant,
plus indexed search inside files. A CLI with a small daemon, a Rust crate,
or an MCP server for coding agents.

```
cargo build --release && ./target/release/fsearch install   # -> ~/.local/bin/fsearch
fsearch fsearch main              # find files by name
fsearch 'ext:rs grep:apply_dir'   # search inside files
```

Or skip the Rust toolchain with a release build for Apple Silicon:

```
curl -L https://github.com/noahdunnagan/fsearch/releases/latest/download/fsearch-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz | tar xz && ./fsearch install
```

## Speed

M4 Mac mini, a home holding the Linux or the Chromium source tree, vs the
previous version (b88f4e9). Medians; Linux / Chromium.

| | before | now |
|---|---:|---:|
| right file first, name search | 83% / 86% | 93% / 97% |
| right file first, two typos | 11% / 15% | 74% / 93% |
| find a file by name | 0.045 / 0.10 ms | 0.054 / 0.12 ms |
| an edited file greppable | 2.1 s | 1.3 ms |
| a rename or delete visible | 45 / 47 ms | 18 / 15 ms |
| first run, a name in a folder | 7.8 / 7.8 s | 0.18 / 1.2 s |
| first run, every match in the tree | 10.9 / 12.2 s | 2.4 / 10.8 s |
| files grep can search (rg's own set) | 96% / 92% | 99.9% / 99.8% |
| grep, first page | 0.29 / 0.48 ms | 0.33 / 0.65 ms |
| index on disk | 503 / 893 MB | 309 / 600 MB |
| peak memory while indexing | 1.13 / 1.37 GB | 0.77 / 0.94 GB |
| daemon memory | 19 / 100 MB | 21 / 35 MB |

The index is a third smaller while holding a third more text: one 3-bit
filter per file instead of two, compressed posting lists and paths, and
bit-packed name arrays read in place. Grep's first page reads a few more
files for it, and the deeper typo search costs a little on names.

## Queries

```
fsearch 'readme in:~/Developer'          # inside a folder
fsearch 'type:image size:>5mb mtime:<7d'
fsearch 'ext:rs regex:fn\s+\w+_dir'      # regex inside files
fsearch 'sym:apply_dir'                  # where it's defined
fsearch 'src/**/*.{c,h} !test/ init'     # globs, in or out
fsearch 'git:modified in:~/Developer/app'
```

Words are fuzzy and forgive a typo at any letter, two in words of 8+
(`mian.rs` finds `main.rs`); several words can spell one name. Accented
names match however they were stored. Also `'exact`, `^prefix`, `suffix$`
and `!exclude`. Filters: `ext:` `type:` `kind:` `in:` `size:` `mtime:`
`re:` `path:` `grep:` `regex:` `sym:` `limit:` and `git:` (`modified`
`staged` `untracked` `clean` `tracked` `ignored` `conflict`). Content search is
smart-case, and regexes match within a line, as in ripgrep.

## What grep covers

Text files up to 1 MB, and up to 10 MB inside git repos, minus what git
ignores. It leaves out lockfiles, JSON of 100 KB and up, minified or
bundled assets, linked git worktrees (their main checkout is indexed), and
build-output folders outside repos. To leave out more, list folders in
`~/Library/Application Support/FSearch/content-skip.txt`, one per line
(`~` and `#` comments work). Names are always indexed, and a grep inside
a file you name still reads it.

## Full Disk Access

From a terminal with Full Disk Access it indexes everything. As a login
item (`fsearch install --login`), grant `~/.local/bin/fsearch` access in
System Settings > Privacy & Security, again after each rebuild. Without
access it skips protected folders instead of prompting.

## API

JSON lines over `~/Library/Application Support/FSearch/fsearch.sock`, or
`fsearch stdio`:

```json
{"q": "fsearch main", "limit": 20, "offset": 20}
{"op": "grep", "pattern": "apply_dir", "in": "~/Developer", "context": 2}
{"q": "main.rs", "boost": true, "near": "~/Developer/app/src/lib.rs", "git": true}
{"op": "open", "path": "~/Developer/app/src/main.rs"}
{"op": "recent", "in": "~/Developer/app"}
```

`open` tells it what you opened; `"boost": true` ranks those higher for a
while, `near` favors files close to the one you're in, and `recent` lists
what you worked on lately. `"git": true` adds each hit's git status.

For coding agents, `fsearch mcp` is an MCP server on stdio with
`find_files`, `grep` and `multi_grep`.

Or link the crate:

```rust
let engine = fsearch::Engine::start(fsearch::Options { dir: fsearch::default_dir(&home), home: home.clone(), skip: None })?;
let hits = engine.search(&fsearch::Query::parse("fsearch main", &home)?)?;
```

An app and the CLI share one index: the first process owns it, the rest
follow.

## How it works

- Crawls the disk once with `getattrlistbulk`, then follows FSEvents:
  changes show up in about 15 ms, and a restart replays only what changed.
  On a first run, a search in a folder indexes that folder first.
- Names live in one mmap'd file, folder by folder, so `in:` is a range. A
  bitmap of each name's letters rules out most names before scoring.
- Content search is a trigram index plus a per-file filter, so a search
  only reads files likely to match. Identical files are indexed once, and
  deleted files' entries are compacted a

# Herdr

Herdr is a desktop app for terminals and coding agents. Keep work in spaces, see which agents need you, and leave terminals running when you close the window.

## Install

### Linux and macOS

```sh
curl -fsSL https://releases.herdr.dev/app/install.sh | sh
```

Linux needs a desktop session and a working Vulkan driver. macOS builds are available for Apple Silicon; Intel Mac users can [build from source](#build-from-source). Linux builds are x86-64 and ARM64.

The installer adds Herdr to your apps and puts the command in `~/.local/bin`.
Add that folder to your PATH if the installer asks.
On macOS the app lives in `~/Applications/Herdr.app`.
For drag-and-drop installation on Apple Silicon, download [Herdr.dmg](https://releases.herdr.dev/app/Herdr.dmg) and drag Herdr to Applications.

On macOS (Apple Silicon), you can also install with [Homebrew](https://brew.sh/):

```sh
brew install --cask herdr-app
```

### Windows

Run in PowerShell on x64 Windows with curl and tar installed (Windows 10 1803 or newer):

```powershell
irm https://releases.herdr.dev/app/install.ps1 | iex
```

Herdr appears in the Start menu. The installer adds `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\herdr-app` to your user PATH. Open a new terminal to pick it up.

The shell and PowerShell installers download and run code. Read the [shell installer](distribution/install.sh) or [PowerShell installer](distribution/install.ps1) first if you prefer.
They also install [herdr-core](https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr-core) if it is missing.
The app can help install or update a core it cannot use.

## Find your work

A **space** holds work on one machine, usually in one repo. Each space has **tabs**. Split a tab into **panes** to put terminals or mod panels beside each other.

An unnamed space follows its first terminal's folder. Name a space or tab when you want a label that stays.
New tabs start in the focused terminal's folder.

The agents sidebar brings agents from your spaces into one list, including workers started by another agent.
Agents that report status show as:

- **Working:** still busy.
- **Blocked:** waiting for you.
- **Done:** finished while you were looking elsewhere.
- **Idle:** not working, or a finished agent you have looked at.

Click an agent to see it. A worker without a pane opens in **peek**, over your tab. Keep it as a tab if you want it beside your other work.
Ctrl-click a live terminal address in terminal text to peek at it; use Cmd-click on macOS.
An address such as `t7` means a terminal on the same machine as the terminal showing it. `vps/t7` names one on another machine.

The window arranges terminals. The core runs them.
Closing the window leaves them running; closing a pane or tab ends its terminals.
After a reboot or core crash, kept panes get fresh shells in their last folders, not their old programs.

## Work on another machine

Add an SSH machine from Settings → Machines or the sidebar's Add machine action.
Pick a host from your SSH config or type how SSH reaches it.
Spaces on that machine run their terminals there, not on your computer.

Each machine keeps its spaces, tabs and splits in its core. Connected screens share that structure and the live terminals, but keep their own focus and zoom.
Remote work keeps running when your local window closes or your laptop sleeps, as long as the remote machine and core stay up.

## Make it yours

Open the command palette to find an action by name, or open Settings to change fonts, colors, sounds and other preferences.
The built-in layouts include Herdr, Terminals and Herdr 98.
A **layout** arranges the window. **Mods** are small JavaScript programs that draw its panels, menus and dialogs.

Duplicate a shipped layout or mod before changing its structure or code. Your copies stay yours; Herdr updates the shipped ones on start.
Save a personal layout, mod or key file and the window reloads it.
A broken edit keeps the last good version and reports the error.

Ctrl+Shift+P shows every command and its key (Cmd+Shift+P on macOS). Change any key in `keys.json`; see [the keys section](defaults/AGENTS.md#keys-keysjson) of the mod guide for the format, including JSON objects for named, typed command arguments.

[Layouts and mods](docs/mods.md) · [Commands](docs/commands.md)

## Updates and privacy

Installed releases check for updates in the background and download a new app beside the running one. It takes over when you quit and reopen, or choose the update action. Your terminals keep running in the core.
Settings → Updates shows what is available. What's New opens after an update; you can open it again from the command palette.
Builds from source do not update themselves.

Usage telemetry is on by default in releases. Turn it off in Settings → Privacy.
Mods are trusted code, not sandboxed extensions. Read [security and privacy](docs/security.md) before installing someone else's mod.

## For agents

```sh
herdr-app --skill
```

This prints the agent guide for driving the window. The herdr-

basic_info.name: blaze
basic_info.description: Incremental rust builds up to 92x faster than cargo/rustc

content.readme:
Rebuild Rust in milliseconds.

Type blaze wherever you'd type cargo.
Blazingly fast Rust, literally.

Install · Try it · How fast · How it works · Docs

## Install ```sh curl -fsSL https://ix.dev/blaze | sh ``` For macOS on Apple silicon and Linux, with or without Rust installed: blaze builds with its own Rust, whatever rustup or the project pins, and the installer downloads it once (about 125 to 160 MB; none when rustup already has that same nightly; v2's blaze cannot fetch it yet: [toolchain.md](docs/toolchain.md)). Rather use crates.io or Nix? [Other ways to install](docs/install.md). That installs **stable**: a release that passed the heavy tests (real projects on macOS and Linux: cargo, zed, servo, bun, NVIDIA Dynamo, fff, fframes, flox and OpenAI's Codex CLI each build, build again after an edit faster than with cargo, and pass their tests). **Canary** is the newest release, out as soon as it is built and promoted to stable unchanged once it passes them ([release.md](docs/release.md)): ```sh curl -fsSL https://ix.dev/blaze | sh -s -- --channel canary ``` ## Try it In any Rust project: ```text blaze run # like cargo run blaze test # like cargo test blaze build # like cargo build ``` The first build loads your project and compiles every crate of it, with no cargo build and no rustc. Then change a function and build again: blaze's daemon, still running, builds only what the edit changed. blaze answers `build`, `check`, `run`, `test` and `bench`; other cargo commands are not blaze's yet. ## How fast These numbers are blaze v1's; v2 has not been measured yet. - Edits rebuild **10× faster** on macOS arm64, **24× faster** on Linux aarch64 and **11× faster** on Linux x86-64 than with `cargo build`, on average over real projects. - **About 20 ms** from saving a file to a running program using the new code, with [live edits](docs/usage.md#change-a-running-program). | Edit one function, then build (Linux x86-64) | `cargo build` | `blaze build` | |---|---:|---:| | ripgrep | 508 ms | **56 ms** (9.1× faster) | | nushell | 1.25 s | **236 ms** (5.3× faster) | | helix | 2.15 s | **116 ms** (19× faster) | | bun (1.25M lines of Rust) | 9.11 s | **451 ms** (20× faster) | Every project, platform, chart, and the memory and disk it takes: [benchmarks](docs/benchmarks.md). ### Over time How blaze's own numbers move from run to run, each platform on its own benchmark machine: the instructions each merge to main retires, how long an edit takes and how soon a live edit runs, from [the history](docs/benchmarks/history) ([how it is kept](docs/benchmarks.md#history-and-regressions)). Every workflow that adds to the history draws these again and commits them with it. Not drawn until there are two runs on one machine: macOS arm64 instructions per merge (none yet), macOS arm64 edit times (one run), Linux aarch64 instructions per merge (none yet), Linux aarch64 edit times (one run), Linux x86-64 instructions per merge (none yet), Linux x86-64 edit times (one run), Windows x86-64 live-edit latency (one run). ## How it works blaze's daemon keeps your project compiled in memory, with no cargo or rustc under it. After an edit it compiles only the functions you changed and links the program again with its own linker. [More](docs/v2/plan.md). ## Good to know - **macOS on Apple silicon and Linux.** Windows has no installer, and v2 has not been run there ([v1 on Windows](docs/platforms.md#windows-x86-64-msvc)). - **blaze is its own toolchain.** It builds every project with its own Rust, `blaze-2026-10-27` (today the nightly of that date), whatever the project pins; stable code and `#![feature(...)]` code build. Your toolchain and CI stay the final word ([why](docs/toolchain.md)). - **It trades memory for speed:** a few GB for a small project. - **It's young.** Keep `cargo check` or your CI as the final word, and [tell us](https://github.com/indexable-inc/blaze/issues) when something

basic_info.name: nsh
basic_info.description: Native Shell is a native UI framework for iOS, Android, macOS, Windows, Linux and the web, built in Rust.

content.readme:
# Native Shell (NSH) **Build once, native everywhere.** Native Shell is a native UI framework for iOS, Android, macOS, Windows, Linux and the web, built in Rust. It unifies components, state, logic and API, with app-owned visual design and platform rendering: native views on iOS, Android, macOS, Windows and Linux, HTML on the web, GPUI in GPUI apps, character Cells in a terminal, with the platform's own text, input and interaction (a menu is a popup on the desktop and a sheet on a phone). Write the whole app in Rust, its screens in TSX, or combine both with shared Rust components. Package it as a standalone app on every platform, or embed it in an existing one. On the same engine, apps load TSX modules at run time — plugins, features, UI generated by AI — delivered as signed packages and run in a sandbox the host configures. Documentation, guides and live demos: **[nsh.dev](https://nsh.dev)**. ## Goals Native views and interaction, with an app-owned design: NSH shares components, state and APIs across platforms, while the app controls colors, typography, spacing, shapes and motion. `nsh/base` provides the behavior and accessible structure of common controls such as `Button`, `Checkbox` and `Switch`; apps and community libraries give them a look. Platform modules expose capabilities specific to their platforms, such as the mobile system tab bar. Read [Goals and design principles](https://nsh.dev/docs/goals) for the component boundaries and how these goals guide Rust apps, TSX modules and AI-generated UI. ## Features - Write apps in Rust, TSX, or both, and render with each platform's own UI, sharing the same reactive engine, flexbox and grid layout, system text, input and accessibility. - Give your app its own look: NSH provides the primitives, Tailwind classes, a theme and an unstyled UI foundation (`nsh/base`: navigation, safe areas, dialogs, the keyboard, the status bar), and your app draws its components from them in TSX or Rust. - Embed in existing native apps alongside components such as maps and web views, or package as standalone apps and static websites. - Deliver TSX screens at run time with signed packages and host-controlled sandbox capabilities. - Build AI-generated screens with TSX and Tailwind, generated TypeScript declarations and [model-readable documentation](https://nsh.dev/llms.txt). - Iterate with TSX hot updates, headless tracing and a single Rust-built `nsh` CLI for building and packaging. ### Platforms | Platform | Drawn with | Embed with | Requires | |---|---|---|---| | iOS | UIKit, CoreText | `NshAppView` (Swift, `NativeShell.xcframework`) | iOS 15+ | | Android | Android views, `StaticLayout` | `NshView` (Java / Kotlin, `nsh.aar`) | Android 9 (API 28)+ | | macOS | AppKit, Core Animation, CoreText | `AppView` (Rust, `nsh-platform-macos`) | macOS 14+ | | Windows | Win32, Direct2D, DirectWrite | `AppView` (Rust, `nsh-platform-windows`) | Windows 10 1809+ | | Linux | GTK 4, Pango | `AppView` (Rust, `nsh-platform-linux`) | GTK 4.14+ | | GPUI (macOS, Windows, Linux) | GPUI (GPUI Fast) | `AppView` (Rust, a GPUI view, `nsh-platform-gpui`) | macOS, Windows; Linux with Vulkan | | Terminal | ratatui, the terminal's Cell grid | `AppView` (Rust, an area of a ratatui frame, `nsh-platform-tui`) | Terminals on macOS, Windows, Linux | | Web | HTML, CSS | `createPlayer` (JavaScript) or an iframe | Modern browsers | Each desktop runs and packages apps with its own backend (AppKit, Win32, GTK 4). The GPUI backend draws with GPUI on all three desktops and embeds NSH in GPUI and GPUI Kit apps; `nsh run --target gpui` shows an app as they do. The web platform (`nsh run --target web`, `nsh package --target web`) publishes apps as static sites and runs the website's live demos. The terminal backend (`nsh run --target tui`) draws apps on a terminal's character grid in its own colors, with the keyboard and the mouse. ## Quick start Install the `nsh` command ([other ways](https://nsh.dev/docs/installation)):
macOS / Linux ```sh curl -fsSL https://nsh.dev/install.sh | sh ``` Build and install the latest `main` from source (Git, Rust and the [platform build dependencies](https://nsh.dev/docs/installation) required): ```sh curl -fsSL https://nsh.dev/install.sh | sh -s -- --source ``` Re-run to update. The checkout stays in `~/.nsh/source` for runtime builds.
Homebrew ```sh brew install longbridge/tap/nsh ```
Windows (PowerShell) ```powershell irm https://nsh.dev/install.ps1 | iex ```
Choose how to write your app: | | Rust | TSX | |---|---|---| | Create | `nsh init my-app --template rust` | `nsh init my-app --template ts` | | Write | Rust components, typed styles and signals | TSX components, Tailwind classes and signals | |

content.readme:
# ts-rust (aka tsc-rs)

I wanted to see if LLMs could port the TypeScript compiler, checker and lsp to Rust. Turns out they can.

It [cost over $420,000](#how-did-this-go) in tokens to do it, but you could probably have done it for ~$20k (see below).

## Benchmark: T3 Code with Effect diagnostics

Full type check of [T3 Code](https://github.com/pingdotgg/t3code) with Effect diagnostics on.\*
Time is the sum of the medians for its five checked projects. Lower is faster. Bar length is
in proportion to time. See [Benchmark: T3 Code](#benchmark-t3-code) for the method and the run
without Effect diagnostics.

| Checker | Time | Relative time | Speed vs tsc 7 |
| --- | ---: | --- | ---: |
| `tsc-rs --fast` | 9.77s | █ | 4.35× |
| `tsc-rs` | 14.30s | ██ | 2.98× |
| `tsc` 7 | 42.55s | █████ | baseline |
| `bun check` | 59.24s | ███████ | 0.72× |
| `tsc` 6 | 191.00s | ████████████████████████ | 0.22× |

\* `tsc-rs` is 0.6.0 with Effect diagnostics built in. `tsc` 7 is from `@effect/tsgo`. The
`bun check` time adds a separate `effect-tsgo diagnostics` run. `tsc` 6 uses the JavaScript
Effect plugin.

## Motivations

- Test model capabilities
- Make a fast TypeScript type checker
- Make a ts checker that can work in WASM with high performance
- Memes

## Warnings

**This is an early release.** It has 100% compatibility in every real world project we have
tested. It should work as a drop in
replacement for the vast majority of apps. See [Known problems](#known-problems).

Also worth mentioning: I've never read a line of this code.

## Install

Be warned, I have no idea if this will actually work.

```sh
npm install -D tsc-rs
npx tsc-rs -p tsconfig.json
```

## How did this go?

I used a lot of OpenAI models to try and complete this port. In total I did **over $400,000 in API priced tokens with GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT 6 Astra**. They wrote over 1.3m lines of Rust over multiple months of /goal loops and never got past like 84% compat.

When I saw how little my Claude Code limits were burning, I figured it'd be fun to throw Opus 5.5 at this. It had a working v0 in 10 hours.

I assumed it kept using the code the Codex models wrote. I was wrong. **Opus 5.5 started from scratch. It got further than Astra in 1/10th the time.**

I let it keep going, and it definitely did. Total token spend was **~$24,047 of API spend over 2 weeks**. I was using my Claude accounts, and it worked out to somewhere between **925% and 983% of my $200 plan weekly limits**.

Expensive, for sure, but not that bad considering how much work has gone into typescript-go.

# "The Slop Line"

Everything below this was written by my LLMs, not me. 

## What actually is this?

ts-rust is a direct port of Microsoft's native TypeScript compiler, which is written in Go
([microsoft/TypeScript](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript), formerly
[typescript-go](https://github.com/microsoft/typescript-go)). It keeps Go's algorithms and
behavior and has the same command line (`tsc`), language server and API.

## Install

```sh
npm install -D tsc-rs
npx tsc-rs -p tsconfig.json
```

`tsc-rs` takes the same options as `tsc`. The npm package is `tsc-rs` so that it does not clash
with the `typescript` package. To use tsc-rs as the `typescript` package (its `tsc` bin, its JS API
and the TypeScript 7 VS Code extension), install
[@tsc-rs/typescript](npm/typescript-readme.md) under that name (from the first release after
0.7.0):

```json
{ "devDependencies": { "typescript": "npm:@tsc-rs/typescript@<version>" } }
```

Each [release](https://github.com/pingdotgg/ts-rust/releases) also has a standalone archive per
platform: the `tsc` binary with the lib files next to it.

Platforms: Linux x64 and arm64 (static, any distribution), macOS arm64, and (from the first
release after 0.2.0) macOS x64, Windows x64 and Windows arm64.

To use it in VS Code, see [@tsc-rs/typescript](npm/typescript-readme.md#vs-code).

## Effect diagnostics

`tsc-rs` has the [Effect](https://effect.website) language service diagnostics built in (codes
377xxx), so an Effect project needs no second compiler. They come from the same check as the
TypeScript diagnostics, and the language server shows them too. They run only when the tsconfig has
the plugin, as with `@effect/language-service`:

```json
{ "compilerOptions": { "plugins": [{ "name": "@effect/language-service" }] } }
```

The rules, options and `@effect-diagnostics` comments are a port of
[Effect-TS/tsgo](https://github.com/Effect-TS/tsgo) 0.51.1. The language server also has its editor
features: the Effect hover (with the Layer summary), inlay hints, the auto-import style, quick fixes,
document symbols, completions and refactors. All the editor features of 0.51.1 are ported. The lightbulb,
the quick fix menu and the editor's Refactor menu show the Effect refactors: as in 0.51.1, the server lists
`refactor.rewrite` in its code action kinds.

The API stability rules of 0.51.1 read the `@stability` JSDoc tags of Effect 4.
